title: Your Worst Post Knows Something
author: Rich Carr
summary: Rich Carr follows up a ten-minute AI quiz exercise for finding blind spots by explaining why people resist it, using a reader's reply that he did not want to know his blind spots. He cites the brain's rapid error signal and the overlap between social threat and physical pain to argue that a miss is filed as a threat before it can be used as information. He ties this to the ostrich effect, in which people avoid useful information about themselves, and calls the habit self-protection with bad aim. Turning to writers, he suggests recording a guess and a confidence rating before publishing, checking stats once a week later, and reading the pattern across five posts. The encouraging half of the argument is hypercorrection: errors made with high confidence are the ones corrected most reliably. He closes with practical habits, such as writing the confidence number down first, and admits he does not want to know his blind spots either.
points: The brain flags an error as a threat within about a tenth of a second, which explains the reluctance to check blind spots even in private.
The ostrich effect shows people avoid useful self-knowledge across money, health and work because a suspected weakness stays negotiable while a confirmed one demands change.
Predicting an outcome and rating confidence before checking results turns raw numbers into feedback that can correct a mental model.
Hypercorrection means the errors people were surest about are the ones they fix best, so the sharpest sting marks the fastest learning.
Practical habits include writing the confidence number first, focusing on misses rated seven or higher, naming the flinch, and rerunning the quiz a week later.
quotes: Your body files a ‘miss’ as a ‘threat’ before your mind gets the chance to file it as information you can use.

A suspected weakness stays negotiable, so you can tell yourself it’s small or something you’ll get to later. A confirmed weakness asks for a change, and change costs energy the brain would rather save.
Self-protection with bad aim is closer to the truth. The brain defends its picture of you, and in doing so it guards you from the exact information that would make the picture accurate.
Five confident misses in the same direction are a blind spot, and your brain is ready to fix it.
The high-confidence misses get fixed, and the fix holds better than any other. The effect is consistent enough to carry a name: hypercorrection.
The miss that stings most is the one you never miss again. Every blind spot you decline to check is a correction your brain was ready to make and never got the chance.
Pay the most attention to anything you rated seven or higher and missed. Those are the misses that rewire.
